newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-AFRICAN VOTES COULD BRING JOHANSSON FIFA PRIZE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-AFRICAN VOTES COULD BRING JOHANSSON FIFA PRIZE.

text.p: If UEFA president Lennart Johansson succeeds Joao Havelange as president of soccer's world governing body FIFA next year, it would be a case of history repeating itself.

The affable 66-year-old Swede has bounced back from a credibility rating of virtually zero after his unfortunate racist remarks about Africans last November to a position of strength -- based on African support.

It was largely African backing which helped Havelange win the FIFA presidency himself in 1974. The Brazilian courted and won his votes with much behind the scenes manoeuvring and promises of increased African representation at future World Cups.

Johansson has also gone for African support, albeit in the full glare of publicity, aligning UEFA, European soccer's governing body, with CAF, their African counterparts, in an historic friendship and sponsorship accord involving a glitzy All Star match and the introduction of a new Under-17 tournament.

All the moves have been done in the open with the avowed aim of developing African soccer. The second half of the notion -- support the Africans and they will support you -- has not been so much as whispered but the intention could hardly have been clearer.
If Johansson does secure the African vote -- and there is still more than a year to go before it will be taken -- he has pulled off a shrewd masterstroke to ensure his political survival.
Apart from the grand political gesture of launching the All Star match and the Under-17 Meridian Cup, he has more importantly set up joint accords between UEFA and CAF.
This initiative, signed on Thursday and known as the Convention, promises extensive co-operation in all football-related matters as well as aid on and off the playing field to the African nations.

The entire package comprising aid, sponsorship, technical help and support to CAF and African national federations, is being compared to the assistance programme UEFA set up to help the former Soviet states in the early 1990s.
Both moves strengthen Johansson's powerbase, helping him first win over the Eastern European nations and now the Africans in his drive to become the most important man in world soccer.
Much can happen between now and when Havelange steps down after next year's World Cup finals in France.

But a number of senior African officials said this week that their votes would probably be cast for Johansson, rather than their own likely candidate Issa Hayatou of Cameroon, a youthful, vigorous man who seems to embody the dynamism of his continent.
But if Hayatou does not win the vote next year, he is unlikely to be disappointed for too long.
The idea that the presidency of FIFA, as well as the venue of future World Cup finals, should be rotated between Europe, Africa, Asia and South America is still a topic for discussion.

As part of a probable deal for backing Johansson, the Africans are likely to insist on a new ruling that would limit the term of office for any future FIFA president to either two or three four-year terms.
This is revolutionary stuff for, once in place, FIFA presidents have historically been in no rush to leave.

By the time he quits office, Havelange, who will be 82 next summer, would have held his autocratic sway over FIFA for 24 years. His English predecessor Sir Stanley Rous was president for 13 years, while the presidency of Jules Rimet of France lasted for 33 years from 1921-54.

Daniel Burley Woolfall of England even technically remained as FIFA president for three years after his death in 1918 -- but that was through no divine intervention, merely a problem created by the confusion in Europe following the First World War.
Johansson seems to have come through a potentially difficult week sitting alongside the Africans with his integrity if not entirely restored then at least not further harmed.
Last November he referred to Africans as "blackies" -- a remark he has admitting making and which he said was meant to be funny though he has since acknowledged it was stupid and ignorant.

Johansson and Hayatou were all smiles and handshakes on Thursday when they signed their new agreement and it was hard to see how Hayatou could seriously challenge the older and vastly more experienced Johansson for the presidency -- even if Hayatou himself still has considerable African support.

Other challengers are believed to be waiting in the wings and the names of current FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter and Italian Franco Carraro, the newly-elected president of the Italian league and a member of the International Olymic Committee have been mentioned.
Johansson however, appears to have redeemed himself this week in Lisbon. If he does win the vote next year, this week could well have proved decisive.
